"""DIN local-activation pooling adapted to UniRank's four-task Taobao schema.

Mechanism references: Zhou et al. DIN (KDD 2018), arXiv:1706.06978;

import torch
from torch import nn
from unirank.pytorch.models import MultiTaskModel
from unirank.pytorch.layers import FeatureEmbeddingDict
from unirank.pytorch.layers.activations import Dice

CONFIG={'embedding_dim':16,'attention_hidden_units':[64,32],
        'tower_hidden_units':[128,64],'attention_normalization':'none'}

    def _coarse_extension_coefficients(self, incumbent, position, quadratic,
                                       linear, rank, scrambled_rank,
                                       valid, counts, total):
        """Replace the redundant fifth direction at fixed learned capacity.

        Event-weighted projection uses the actual validity mask, including
        partial/noncontiguous blocks. Every candidate coefficient is block
        constant on valid events, hence orthogonal to the first target-match
        and second local-position coefficients as well. A common gate and
        norm make information content the main replacement contrast. The
        gate can itself carry information; the duplicate isolates that.
        """
        cubic = self._coarse_residual(
            rank * rank * rank, linear, quadratic, valid, total)
        scrambled = self._coarse_residual(
            scrambled_rank * scrambled_rank * scrambled_rank,
            linear, quadratic, valid, total)
        cubic_norm2 = cubic.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        scrambled_norm2 = scrambled.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        incumbent_norm2 = incumbent.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        target_norm2 = position.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        occupied = (counts > 0).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
        support = ((occupied >= 4) & (cubic_norm2 > 1e-10)
                   & (scrambled_norm2 > 1e-10)
                   & (incumbent_norm2 > 1e-10)
                   & (target_norm2 > 1e-10)).to(valid.dtype)
        cubic = (cubic * (target_norm2 / cubic_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt()
                 * support)
        scrambled = (scrambled
                     * (target_norm2 / scrambled_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt()
                     * support)
        duplicate = incumbent * support
        # All alternatives above execute in all cells; no modules or RNG added.
        if self.coarse_extension == 'cubic':
            return cubic
        if self.coarse_extension == 'scrambled':
            return scrambled
        if self.coarse_extension == 'duplicate':
            return duplicate

    @staticmethod
    def _coarse_residual(raw, linear, quadratic, valid, total):
        """Two projection sweeps in FP32; zero bases are harmless."""
        residual = valid * raw
        linear_norm2 = linear.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        quadratic_norm2 = quadratic.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        for _ in range(2):
            mean = residual.sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
            residual = valid * (residual - mean)
            slope = ((residual * linear).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
                     / linear_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12))
            residual = valid * (residual - slope * linear)
            slope = ((residual * quadratic).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
                     / quadratic_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12))
            residual = valid * (residual - slope * quadratic)
        mean = residual.sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
        return valid * (residual - mean)

    def _joint_coefficients(self, affinity, position, fourth, valid, counts,
                            rank, scrambled_rank):
        """Retain the incumbent gate; vary only duplicate-match support/scale.

        All basis construction is FP32 and independent of learned values.
        Within-block centering gives orthogonality to every block-constant
        coefficient, including the inherited linear and quadratic moments.
        Two projection sweeps reduce finite-precision leakage into the
        remaining local-ordinal and target-match directions. The common
        support gate can carry availability information even in a duplicate
        direction. Build every inherited coefficient in all factorial cells;
        basic availability additionally admits matches lacking joint moments.
        """
        position_norm2 = position.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        match_norm2 = affinity.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        fourth_norm2 = fourth.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        # Orthogonalize affinity against position first. A zero basis is
        # harmless; no inverse of a near-singular two-by-two matrix is used.
        basis = affinity
        for _ in range(2):
            slope = ((basis * position).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
                     / position_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10))
            basis = valid * (basis - slope * position)
            basis = valid * (basis - basis.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
                             / counts.clamp_min(1))
        basis_norm2 = basis.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        basis = basis * (basis_norm2 > 1e-10).to(valid.dtype)
        basis_norm2 = basis.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)

        ordered = self._joint_residual(
            affinity * rank, position, position_norm2,
            basis, basis_norm2, valid, counts)
        scrambled = self._joint_residual(
            affinity * scrambled_rank, position, position_norm2,
            basis, basis_norm2, valid, counts)
        ordered_norm2 = ordered.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        scrambled_norm2 = scrambled.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
        support = ((ordered_norm2 > 1e-10) & (scrambled_norm2 > 1e-10)
                   & (position_norm2 > 1e-10) & (match_norm2 > 1e-10)
                   & (fourth_norm2 > 1e-10)).to(valid.dtype)
        ordered = ordered * (position_norm2 / ordered_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt() * support
        scrambled = scrambled * (position_norm2 / scrambled_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt() * support
        duplicate_match = affinity * (position_norm2 / match_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt() * support
        duplicate_curvature = fourth * (position_norm2 / fourth_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt() * support

        # and positions. No labels, learned values, new state or RNG enter.
        available = ((position_norm2 > 1e-10)
                     & (match_norm2 > 1e-10)).to(valid.dtype)
        available_norm = affinity * (position_norm2 / match_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt() * available

        joint_raw = affinity * support

        # returns exactly the old expression for a same-seed parity bridge.
        if self.match_support == 'available':

    @staticmethod
    def _joint_residual(raw, position, position_norm2, basis, basis_norm2, valid, counts):
        residual = valid * (raw - (raw * valid).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
                            / counts.clamp_min(1))
        for _ in range(2):

                     / position_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10))
            residual = valid * (residual - slope * position)
            slope = ((residual * basis).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
                     / basis_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10))
            residual = valid * (residual - slope * basis)
            residual = valid * (residual - residual.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
                                / counts.clamp_min(1))
        return residual

    @staticmethod
    def _orthogonal_block_residual(raw, linear, linear_norm2, valid, total):
        mean = (raw * valid).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
        residual = valid * (raw - mean)
        slope = ((residual * linear).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
                 / linear_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12))
        residual = valid * (residual - slope * linear)
        # Recenter once more to reduce finite-precision constant leakage.
        residual_mean = residual.sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
        residual = valid * (residual - residual_mean)
        return residual, residual.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)

    def _compress_both(self, values, mask, auxiliary):
        batch, length, width = values.shape
        if length != 100:
            raise ValueError('Frozen protocol requires 100 history positions')
        groups, block_size = 10, 10
        valid = mask.bool().reshape(batch, groups, block_size)
        membership = auxiliary.reshape(batch, groups, block_size) & valid
        # Per temporal block: one uniform slot and two feedback strata.
        # Each branch independently covers every valid event exactly once.
        assignment = torch.stack((valid, valid & ~membership, membership), dim=-2)
        assignment = assignment.to(values.dtype).reshape(batch * groups, 3, block_size)
        counts = assignment.sum(-1)
        grouped = values.reshape(batch * groups, block_size, width)
        sums = torch.bmm(assignment, grouped)
        means = sums / counts.clamp_min(1).unsqueeze(-1)
        return means.reshape(batch, groups * 3, width), counts.reshape(batch, groups * 3)

    def _compress_with_match(self, values, mask, auxiliary, match_union):
        """Seven rows with population-matched counts and support emptiness.

        Valid-rank rotation operates inside a block, including noncontiguous
        validity masks, and preserves target-match cardinality. Special IDs
        have already been excluded by _target_match_summary. No labels,
        external identities, timestamps, state or RNG enter this assignment.
        """
        batch, length, width = values.shape
        if length != 100:
            raise ValueError('Frozen protocol requires 100 history positions')
        valid = mask.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10)
        feedback = auxiliary.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10) & valid
        matched = match_union.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10) & valid
        rotated = self._rotate_valid_membership(matched, valid)
        # Both support pairs have identical per-block cardinalities and
        # empty-slot patterns. Duplicate control removes only aligned value
        # grouping; the target-match counts and rotated pair remain present.
        first_support = (matched if self.normalization_support == 'aligned_rotated'
                         else rotated)
        assignment = torch.stack(
            (valid, valid & ~feedback, feedback,
             valid & ~first_support, first_support,
             valid & ~rotated, rotated), dim=-2)
        assignment = assignment.to(values.dtype).reshape(batch * 10, 7, 10)
        counts = assignment.sum(dim=-1)
        sums = torch.bmm(assignment, values.reshape(batch * 10, 10, width))
        means = sums / counts.clamp_min(1).unsqueeze(-1)
        return means.reshape(batch, 70, width), counts.reshape(batch, 70)

    @staticmethod
    def _rotate_valid_membership(matched, valid):
        # Pack membership by valid-event rank, rotate by half the valid
        # count, then unpack to the original valid positions. Invalid
        # entries contribute zero even when scatter indices coincide.
        matched = matched & valid
        ranks = (valid.long().cumsum(dim=-1) - 1).clamp_min(0)
        counts = valid.long().sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        packed = torch.zeros_like(ranks).scatter_add(-1, ranks, matched.long())
        source = (ranks + counts // 2).remainder(counts.clamp_min(1))
        return packed.gather(-1, source).bool() & valid

    def _pool_seven(self, weights, values, counts):
        batch = values.shape[0]
        weights = weights.reshape(batch, 70) * counts.to(weights.dtype)
        weighted = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) * values).reshape(
            batch, 10, 7, self.value_width)
        return weighted.sum(dim=1)

    def _interactions(self, target, values):
        keys = values[:, :, :self.key_width]
        action = values[:, :, self.key_width:]
        batch, slots, _ = keys.shape
        query = target[:, None, :].expand(-1, slots, -1)
        return torch.cat([query, keys, query - keys, query * keys, action], dim=-1).reshape(batch * slots, -1)

    def _primary_activation(self, interactions):
        """Forward-identical stop-gradient on nonreadout support rows.

        Flattened order is batch, block, seven strata. The first three strata
        retain the incumbent gradient paths. Before EACH Dice, rows 3..6
        become constants for moment estimation in the blocked cell. This
        removes their backward contribution to the preceding affine layer
        and embedding sources, while preserving their forward activations,
        batch moments and running-buffer updates at a fixed parameter state.
        Selected rows still differentiate through their own batch moments;
        shared scorer parameters and later updates can consequently differ.
        No extra scorer pass, parameters, persistent state or RNG is added.
        """
        if not self.training or self.support_gradient == 'attached':
            return self.local_activation(interactions)
        retained = (torch.arange(interactions.shape[0], device=interactions.device)
                    .remainder(7) < 3).unsqueeze(-1)
        hidden = interactions
        for layer in self.local_activation:
            if isinstance(layer, Dice):
                hidden = torch.where(retained, hidden, hidden.detach())
            hidden = layer(hidden)
        return hidden

    def _auxiliary_activation(self, interactions):
        # Functional evaluation uses the SAME learned scorer with parameter
        # stop-gradient fixed on. Do not use no_grad: gradients into each
        # allowed embedding source must survive the shared scoring operator.
        parameters = {
            name: (parameter.detach() if self.block_aux_scorer_grad else parameter)
            for name, parameter in self.local_activation.named_parameters()
        }
        # Dice contains BatchNorm running state. Only the primary call may
        # update persistent buffers. Cloned auxiliary buffers also prevent an
        # in-place second update of state referenced by the first graph.
        buffers = {name: buffer.detach().clone()
                   for name, buffer in self.local_activation.named_buffers()}
        return torch.func.functional_call(
            self.local_activation, (parameters, buffers), (interactions,), strict=True)

"""Registered public evidence access; no arbitrary host paths or private sources."""
import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
import time

from knowledge_engine import retrieve,rank,REVISION

ROOT=Path('/workspace')


def safe_path(relative):
    path=(ROOT/relative).resolve()
    if not path.is_relative_to(ROOT.resolve()) or not path.is_file():
        raise ValueError('Reference is outside the authorized public workspace')
    return path


def registered(reference):
    registry=json.loads((ROOT/'registry.json').read_text())
    if reference not in registry:raise ValueError('Unknown authorized reference: '+reference)
    entry=registry[reference]
    return {'json':entry} if isinstance(entry,str) else entry


def access(operation,**values):
    with (ROOT/'knowledge-access.jsonl').open('a') as stream:
        stream.write(json.dumps({'revision':REVISION,'operation':operation,'at_unix':time.time(),**values},ensure_ascii=False)+'\n')


def execute(operation,reference=None,query=None,source=None,top=6,find=None,start_line=1,lines=100):
    if operation=='search':
        cards=[json.loads(line) for line in (ROOT/'evidence.jsonl').read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]
        if source:
            rows=rank(cards,query,source=source)[:max(1,min(top,6))]
            result={'revision':REVISION,'query':query,'source':source,'matches':[row['card'] for row in rows],
                    'scores':[{key:row[key] for key in ['id','knowledge_type','score','indexed_tokens']} for row in rows]}
        else:
            result=retrieve(cards,query,limit=max(1,min(top,6)))
            result['matches']=result.pop('cards')
        access(operation,query=query,source=source,matched_ids=[card['id'] for card in result['matches']])
        return result
    entry=registered(reference)
    metadata=json.loads(safe_path(entry['json']).read_text())
    if operation=='resolve':
        access(operation,reference=reference,source_id=metadata.get('id'),version=metadata.get('version'),text_sha256=metadata.get('text_sha256'))
        return metadata
    if operation!='read':raise ValueError('Unknown capability')
    if 'text' not in entry:
        if metadata.get('fallback_ref'):
            access(operation,reference=reference,status='no_detailed_text',fallback_ref=metadata['fallback_ref'])
            return {'id':metadata.get('id'),'status':'Detailed text unavailable; read the explicitly labeled fallback',
                    'fallback_ref':metadata['fallback_ref'],'access_scope':metadata.get('access_scope')}
        content=json.dumps(metadata,ensure_ascii=False,indent=2)
    else:content=safe_path(entry['text']).read_text()
    values=content.splitlines();begin=max(0,start_line-1);count=max(1,min(lines,160))
    if find:
        matches=[i for i,line in enumerate(values) if find.casefold() in line.casefold()]
        if not matches:
            access(operation,reference=reference,find=find,status='no_match')
            return {'id':metadata.get('id'),'status':'no matching text','total_lines':len(values)}
        begin=max(0,next((i for i in matches if i>=begin),matches[0])-2)
    selected=values[begin:begin+count]
    bounded='\n'.join(f'{begin+i+1}: {line}' for i,line in enumerate(selected))
    clipped=len(bounded)>24000
    access(operation,reference=reference,source_id=metadata.get('id'),version=metadata.get('version'),
           text_sha256=metadata.get('text_sha256'),start_line=begin+1,lines=len(selected),truncated=clipped,find=find)
    return {'id':metadata.get('id'),'url':metadata.get('url'),'version':metadata.get('version'),
            'access_scope':metadata.get('access_scope'),'text_sha256':metadata.get('text_sha256'),
            'total_lines':len(values),'start_line':begin+1,'next_line':begin+len(selected)+1,
            'truncated':clipped,'text':bounded[:24000]}


def main():
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser();sub=parser.add_subparsers(dest='operation',required=True)
    for name in ['resolve','read']:
        command=sub.add_parser(name);command.add_argument('reference')
        if name=='read':
            command.add_argument('--find');command.add_argument('--start-line',type=int,default=1)
            command.add_argument('--lines',type=int,default=100)
    command=sub.add_parser('search');command.add_argument('query',nargs='+')
    command.add_argument('--source',choices=['paper','industry','agent']);command.add_argument('--top',type=int,default=6)
    args=vars(parser.parse_args())
    if 'query' in args:args['query']=' '.join(args['query'])
    print(json.dumps(execute(**args),ensure_ascii=False,indent=2))


if __name__=='__main__':main()

232: Pooling layer and Concat layer
233: Notice that different users have different numbers of behaviors. Thus the number of non-zero values for multi-hot behavioral feature vector 𝒕i\bm{t}_{i} varies across instances, causing the lengths of the corresponding list of embedding vectors to be variable.
234: As fully connected networks can only handle fixed-length inputs, it is a common practice (et al., 2016a; Covington
235: et al., 2016) to transform the list of embedding vectors via a pooling layer to get a fixed-length vector:
236: (1)

238: Two most commonly used pooling layers are sum pooling and average pooling, which apply element-wise sum/average operations to the list of embedding vectors.
239: Both embedding and pooling layers operate in a group-wise manner, mapping the original sparse features into multiple fixed-length representation vectors.
240: Then all the vectors are concatenated together to obtain the overall representation vector for the instance.
241: MLP
242: Given the concatenated dense representation vector, fully connected layers are used to learn the combination of features automatically.
243: Recently developed methods (et al., 2016a; Guo
244: et al., 2017; et al., 2016b) focus on designing structures of MLP for better information extraction.
245: Loss
246: The objective function used in base model is the negative log-likelihood function defined as:
247: (2)
248: L=−1N∑(𝒙,y)∈𝒮(ylogp(𝒙)+(1−y)log(1−p(𝒙))),L=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{(\bm{x},y)\in\mathcal{S}}(y\log p(\bm{x})+(1-y)\log(1-p(\bm{x}))),
249: where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the training set of size NN, with 𝒙\bm{x} as the input of the network and y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} as the label, p⁡(𝒙)p(\bm{x}) is the output of the network after the softmax layer, representing the predicted probability of sample 𝒙\bm{x} being clicked.
250: 4.3. The structure of Deep Interest Network
251: Among all those features of Table 1, user behavior features are critically important and play key roles in modeling user interests in the scenario of e-commerce applications.
252: Base model obtains a fixed-length representation vector of user interests by pooling all the embedding vectors over the user behavior feature group, as Eq.(1). This representation vector stays the same for a given user, in regardless of what candidate ads are.
253: In this way, the user representation vector with a limited dimension will be a bottleneck to express user’s diverse interests.
254: To make it capable enough, an easy method is to expand the dimension of embedding vector, which unfortunately will increase the size of learning parameters heavily.
255: It will lead to overfitting under limited training data and add the burden of computation and storage, which may not be tolerated for an industrial online system.
256: Is there an elegant way to represent user’s diverse interests in one vector under limited dimension?
257: The local activation characteristic of user interests gives us inspiration to design a novel model named deep interest network(DIN).
258: Imagine when the young mother mentioned above in section 3 visits the e-commerce site, she finds the displayed new handbag cute and clicks it.
259: Let’s dissect the driving force of click action.
260: The displayed ad hits the related interests of this young mother by soft-searching her historical behaviors and finding that she had browsed similar goods of tote bag and leather handbag recently.
261: In other words, behaviors related to displayed ad greatly contribute to the click action.
262: DIN simulates this process by paying attention to the representation of locally activated interests w.r.t. given ad.
263: Instead of expressing all user’s diverse interests with the same vector, DIN adaptively calculate the representation vector of user interests by taking into consideration the relevance of historical behaviors w.r.t. candidate ad.
264: This representation vector varies over different ads.
265: The right part of Fig.2 illustrates the architecture of DIN.
266: Compared with base model, DIN introduces a novel designed local activation unit and maintains the other structures the same. Specifically, activation units are applied on the user behavior features, which performs as a weighted sum pooling to adaptively calculate user representation 𝒗U\bm{v}_{U} given a candidate ad AA, as shown in Eq.(3)
267: (3)
268: 𝒗U(A)=f(𝒗A,𝒆1,𝒆2,..,𝒆H)=∑j=1Ha⁡(𝒆j,𝒗A)​𝒆j=∑j=1H𝒘j​𝒆j,\displaystyle\begin{split}\bm{v}_{U}(A)=f(\bm{v}_{A},\bm{e}_{1},\bm{e}_{2},..,\bm{e}_{H})&=\sum_{j=1}^{H}a(\bm{e}_{j},\bm{v}_{A})\bm{e}_{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{H}\bm{w}_{j}\bm{e}_{j},\end{split}
269: where {𝒆1,𝒆2,…,𝒆H}\{\bm{e}_{1},\bm{e}_{2},...,\bm{e}_{H}\} is the list of embedding vectors of behaviors of user UU with length of HH, 𝒗A\bm{v}_{A} is the embedding vector of ad AA. In this way, 𝒗U​(A)\bm{v}_{U}(A) varies over different ads. a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot) is a feed-forward network with output as the activation weight, as illustrated in Fig.2. Apart from the two input embedding vectors, a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot) adds the out product of them to feed into the subsequent network, which is an explicit knowledge to help relevance modeling.
270: Local activation unit of Eq.(3) shares similar ideas with attention methods which are developed in NMT task(Bahdanau
271: et al., 2015).
272: However different from traditional attention method, the constraint of ∑iwi=1\sum_{i}w_{i}=1 is relaxed in Eq.(3), aiming to reserve the intensity of user interests.
273: That is, normalization with softmax on the output of a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot) is abandoned.
274: Instead, value of ∑iwi\sum_{i}w_{i} is treated as an approximation of the intensity of activated user interests to some degree.
275: For example, if one user’s historical behaviors contain 90% clothes and 10% electronics.
276: Given two candidate ads of T-shirt and phone, T-shirt activates most of the historical behaviors belonging to clothes and may get larger value of 𝒗U\bm{v}_{U} (higher intensity of interest) than phone.
277: Traditional attention methods lose the resolution on the numerical scale of 𝒗U\bm{v}_{U} by normalizing of the output of a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot).
278: We have tried LSTM to model user historical behavior data in the sequential manner.
279: But it shows no improvement.
280: Different from text which is under the constraint of grammar in NLP task, the sequence of user historical behaviors may contain multiple concurrent interests.
281: Rapid jumping and sudden ending over these interests causes the sequence data of user behaviors to seem to be noisy.
282: A possible direction is to design special structures to model such data in a sequence way.
283: We leave it for future research.
284: 5. Training Techniques
285: In the advertising system in Alibaba, numbers of goods and users scale up to hundreds of millions.
286: Practically, training industrial deep networks with large scale sparse input features is of great challenge.
287: In this section, we introduce two important techniques which are proven to be helpful in practice.
288: 5.1. Mini-batch Aware Regularization
289: Overfitting is a critical challenge for training industrial networks.
290: For example, with addition of fine-grained features, such as features of goods_ids with dimensionality of 0.6 billion (including v​i​s​i​t​e​d​_​g​o​o​d​s​_​i​d​svisited\_goods\_ids of user and g​o​o​d​s​_​i​dgoods\_id of ad as described in Table 1), model performance falls rapidly after the first epoch during training without regularization, as the dark green line shown in Fig.4 in later section 6.5.
291: It is not practical to directly apply traditional regularization methods, such as ℓ2\ell_{2} and ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization, on training networks with sparse inputs and hundreds of millions of parameters.
292: Take ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization as an example.
293: Only parameters of non-zero sparse features appearing in each mini-batch needs to be updated in the scenario of SGD based optimization methods without regularization.
294: However, when adding ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization it needs to calculate L2-norm over the whole parameters for each mini-batch, which leads to extremely heavy computations and is unacceptable with parameters scaling up to hundreds of millions.
295: Figure 3. Control function of PReLU and Dice.
